entries.title: The Semantic Cost of Instant Understanding
entries.description:

The phrase "I understand" is so common in English that we barely notice it, yet its literal meaning is surprisingly spatial: to stand under or among. This linguistic quirk, rooted in Old Norse, suggests an early conceptualization of comprehension as being immersed in or supported by something. Contrast this with "comprehend," which comes from Latin and implies grasping or seizing. Our everyday language, therefore, offers us two distinct, almost physical metaphors for making sense of the world.
